Describe the problems facing the Soviet Union when Gorbachev came to power in 1985.

points.description: A stagnating economy falling behind the West in technology and living standards.
The cost of the arms race, made worse by Reagan's Strategic Defence Initiative.
The costly and unwinnable war in Afghanistan (from 1979).
The cost of supporting Eastern Europe / discontent in the satellites.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The Soviet economy was stagnating and falling behind the West in technology and living standards. Military spending took a large share of national wealth, and Reagan's plans for space-based missile defence threatened a costly new arms race. The war in Afghanistan, begun in 1979, was costing lives and money and could not be won, and the USSR was also paying to support the struggling economies of Eastern Europe.

stem: Explain why Solidarity was a threat to the Polish communist government.

points.description: Identifies its size (about ten million members).
Explains that a workers' movement outside the party challenged the party's claim to represent the workers.
Identifies its independence / links with the Church.
Explains that it offered an alternative source of loyalty and could organise national strikes, and the USSR feared it would spread.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Solidarity had about ten million members, roughly a third of the working-age population, and it was a movement of workers outside the Communist Party, which undermined the party's claim to rule on behalf of the workers. It was independent and closely linked with the Catholic Church, so it offered an alternative focus of loyalty and could paralyse the country with strikes; the USSR feared that its example would spread to other satellites.

hints: Whom did the Communist Party claim to represent?

stem: Explain why communist rule collapsed in Eastern Europe in 1989.

points.description: Identifies Gorbachev's refusal to use force / abandonment of the Brezhnev Doctrine.
Explains that without the threat of Soviet tanks, governments could not suppress protest as in 1956 and 1968.
Identifies economic failure and debt.
Explains that falling living standards undermined support, and Western television showed a richer life.
Identifies popular movements (Solidarity, Leipzig demonstrations, Velvet Revolution).
Explains that Poland's example in June 1989 showed change was possible, and protest spread from country to country.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The most immediate reason was Gorbachev's refusal to use force: once the Brezhnev Doctrine was abandoned, communist governments could no longer rely on Soviet tanks, as they had in 1956 and 1968. Underlying this was economic failure: the satellites were in debt, living standards were falling, and Western television showed people a richer life, so few people supported the regimes. Finally, popular movements took the chance: Solidarity's victory in the Polish elections of June 1989 showed that change was possible, and mass protests spread to Leipzig, Berlin and Prague, bringing down one government after another.

hints: Moscow, the economy and the people.

**Source A** — the memoir of a fictional Polish shipyard worker, published in 1995 (invented for this question)

> When we struck at the shipyard, we did not ask for the moon. We asked for a union of our own, a monument to the workers shot ten years before, and the truth on the radio. When they gave us the union, ten million people joined. After that, martial law could lock us up, but it could not make us forget.

**Source B** — a cartoon of the kind published in Western European newspapers in November 1989, described in words (described in words; invented for this question)

> A row of statues of communist leaders is toppling like dominoes, from one labelled "Warsaw" to one labelled "Prague". At the side, a smiling man with a birthmark on his forehead stands with his hands in his pockets, whistling, and does nothing to stop them.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Source A is useful because it is the view of a participant, showing why Polish workers joined Solidarity and how martial law failed to crush it. But it was written in 1995, with hindsight and pride, and it covers only Poland. Source B is useful because it shows the domino effect of 1989, with regimes falling from Warsaw to Prague, and Gorbachev standing by. My own knowledge supports this: after Solidarity's victory in June 1989, Hungary opened its border, the Wall was opened in November and the Velvet Revolution followed, while Gorbachev refused to use force. However, a cartoon simplifies, and neither source mentions economic failure, debt or pressure from the West. Together the sources are useful for showing the roles of people power and Gorbachev, but they need own knowledge to give a full explanation.

parts.explanation: Use content, provenance and own knowledge.

hints: Each source gives the credit for change to different people.

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
Gorbachev played a decisive part. In 1956 and 1968 the USSR had crushed reform by force, but Gorbachev made clear that he would not do so: he accepted Solidarity's victory in Poland in 1989 and kept Soviet troops in their barracks in East Germany. His policies of glasnost and perestroika also encouraged people in the satellites to demand similar reforms.

However, he did not create the problems. The Soviet and Eastern European economies had been stagnating for years, the satellites were in debt, and the war in Afghanistan and the arms race, pushed further by Reagan's plans for missile defence, drained resources. These pressures were why Gorbachev needed reform in the first place. The collapse was also the work of the people of Eastern Europe: Solidarity had survived martial law, and in 1989 the crowds in Leipzig, Berlin and Prague forced their governments out.

Gorbachev was personally responsible for the timing and peaceful character of the collapse, because a different leader might have used force. But the long-term causes were economic failure and the lack of popular support, so he was a necessary trigger rather than the sole cause.
